nameStory: The zebra clubtail gets its striking name from the bold black and yellow stripes that run along its abdomen, creating a pattern reminiscent of a zebra's markings. Like all clubtails, it has a distinctive swollen tip at the end of its abdomen that resembles a tiny club. This zebra-striped club makes it one of the most recognizable dragonflies along New England's waterways.
description: The zebra clubtail is a medium-sized dragonfly that's part of the clubtail family, known for their characteristic swollen abdominal tips. These impressive insects have bold black and yellow striped abdomens and clear wings that they hold perpendicular to their bodies when at rest. Adults typically measure about 2-3 inches in length with a wingspan reaching nearly 4 inches. They're powerful fliers that patrol rivers and streams, often perching on rocks, logs, or bare ground along the water's edge.

idTips.label: Zebra-striped abdomen
idTips.description: Look for the unmistakable alternating black and yellow bands running down the length of the abdomen - they're bold and crisp like a zebra's stripes, not faded or blurry

idTips.label: Clubbed tail tip
idTips.description: The end of the abdomen flares out into a noticeable bulge or 'club' that feels firm if gently touched - this swollen tip distinguishes all clubtails from other dragonfly families

idTips.label: Clear wings
idTips.description: Wings are completely transparent with fine black veining, lacking any colored patches or smoky areas that you might see on other dragonfly species

idTips.label: Yellow-green eyes
idTips.description: The large compound eyes have a bright yellow-green color that almost seems to glow in sunlight, and they're positioned widely apart on the head

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Often seen resting flat on sun-warmed rocks, bare soil, or wooden surfaces near water with wings held straight out from the body - they rarely hang vertically like some other dragonflies

habitat: Zebra clubtails are found along clean, flowing rivers and larger streams throughout New England, particularly favoring areas with rocky or sandy bottoms. They prefer waters with moderate current and good water quality, often seen near riffles and shallow areas where the water runs clear over stones. You'll typically spot adults perching on exposed rocks, gravel bars, or sunny patches of bare ground within 50 feet of the water's edge.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their aquatic larval stage in late May, with peak emergence happening in early June when you might find empty larval shells (exuvia) clinging to rocks near the water's edge.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs from mid-June through August when adults are actively hunting, mating, and laying eggs - this is the best time to observe their distinctive zebra stripes and territorial behavior along waterways.
seasonality.fall: Activity winds down significantly by September, though a few stragglers may be seen into early October on particularly warm days before the first hard frosts end the flight season.
seasonality.winter: No adults are present - the species overwinters as larvae (nymphs) buried in the muddy or sandy bottom of streams and rivers, slowly developing for the next year's emergence.

funFact: Zebra clubtail larvae are underground architects that can take up to 4 years to develop, spending most of that time buried in stream sediments like living bulldozers, using their powerful legs to dig through sand and gravel while hunting for prey with lightning-fast extending jaws.
confusionNotes: The zebra clubtail's bold striped pattern makes it fairly distinctive, but it can be confused with other clubtails in the same genus - remember the mnemonic 'Zebra = Ztripes' to focus on those crisp, contrasting black and yellow bands that are much bolder than the more subtle markings on arrow or riverine clubtails.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'clubtails,' these dragonflies don't use their swollen tail tips as weapons - the club is actually expanded reproductive structures and is more pronounced in males than females, helping experts determine the sex of individuals in the field.
compareHints: Among its hanging clubtail relatives, the zebra clubtail stands out with its bold, high-contrast striped pattern - the arrow clubtail has more muted markings with arrow-like shapes rather than stripes, while the riverine clubtail shows more olive-brown coloration with less distinct banding. If you can clearly see zebra-like stripes from several feet away, you're likely looking at a zebra clubtail rather than its more subtly marked cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Arrow Clubtails are distinguished from their Zebra Clubtail cousins by the arrow marking versus zebra-like stripes, and from Riverine Clubtails by their preference for larger streams rather than small headwater brooks.
